score_rationale: The verified core contribution is real and potentially useful, but the manuscript needs sharper scope control, fuller comparison to adjacent work, and clearer exposition of the strong design assumptions before it earns publication in a leading econometrics journal.
summary: The paper studies honest expected length for confidence sets for transported complier ratios under weak first stages, with a compact causal range and an effective-strength index n mu_n^2/kappa_n. The verified results deliver matched rate-order lower and upper bounds for oracle procedures, fixed-geometry slices, and feasible finite-cell weight learning under the stated cell designs. The contribution is mathematically coherent and novel in its combination of transport weighting and weak-ratio inference, but the current manuscript sometimes presents rate-order results as a full frontier characterization and gives too little comparative detail on the closest econometric benchmarks.
strengths: The central effective-strength index n mu_n^2/kappa_n is clean and economically interpretable.
The compact causal range is used productively to obtain finite expected-length behavior in weak-first-stage regimes.
The oracle lower and upper bounds, fixed-geometry refinement, and finite-cell feasible constructions form a coherent theorem sequence.
The assumptions and formal statements are unusually explicit, and the verified statements support the main mathematical claims.

findings.issue: Several high-level sentences make the contribution sound like an exact characterization of expected length rather than a rate-order characterization under fixed thresholds and specific procedure classes. Offending sentences include: 'This paper characterizes the honest expected length of confidence sets for the transported complier ratio.' and 'Together, the oracle, no-shift, and fixed-geometry results characterize honest minimax expected length for the transported complier ratio as a function of the effective-strength threshold.' The verified statements give two-sided bounds up to constants for fixed t0, plus finite-cell feasible extensions under stated cell designs.
findings.fix: Rewrite the overview and discussion to say that the paper characterizes the minimax expected-length rate order, up to constants, for fixed effective-strength thresholds under the stated oracle, fixed-geometry, uniform finite-cell, and known regular-cell classes.

findings.issue: The related-work section is broad and well cited, but it gives limited direct comparison to the closest results' objects, rates, assumptions, and inferential guarantees. The most relevant comparisons are Chen and Huang on transported CACE estimation, Choi-Gu-Shen and Choi-Shen on two-sample weak IV, Ma and Smucler-Lanni-Masip on weak-LATE confidence sets, and Zeng-Kennedy-Bodnar-Naimi on transported ATE minimax theory.
findings.fix: Add a focused comparison paragraph or table listing the target estimand, whether transport weights are known or learned, whether first stages may be weak, whether the parameter space is compact, and the inferential guarantee/rate. Use it to locate the new contribution affirmatively against each benchmark.

findings.issue: The strong design restrictions that make the feasible results work are stated formally but receive little econometric motivation: uniform source cells with mass 1/k_n, balanced assignment in the uniform finite-cell class, known q_{x,n} and known cell-varying propensity in the regular class, and k_n=o(sqrt n). A reader needs to understand when these are design features, approximations, or technical regimes.
findings.fix: Add a short assumptions subsection after the model definitions explaining concrete designs covered by each feasible class, why the sub-root cell growth condition appears, and how the regular-cell result should be interpreted when q and e are supplied by the sampling frame or randomization design.

findings.issue: The term 'sample-only' is potentially ambiguous. The abstract says 'empirical target cell frequencies yield a sample-only score inversion attaining the same order,' while the regular extension explicitly uses known source-cell probabilities and known propensity, and the uniform construction still relies on the observed common cell labels and balanced assignment design.
findings.fix: Define 'sample-only' at first use as excluding oracle transport weights, and state the design inputs separately: common finite-cell labels and balanced propensity for the uniform class; known q_{x,n} and e(x) for the regular class.

findings.issue: The proof of the finite-cell theorem invokes the regular-cell theorem before the latter is proved, and the appendix gives long low-level verification-style proofs without an early dependency map. This makes the argument harder to audit as an econometrics paper, even though the formal proof is verified.
findings.fix: Add a short proof roadmap at the start of the appendix and either reorder the main-result proofs so dependencies run forward or explicitly state that the finite-cell theorem is derived as a corollary of the later regular-cell theorem with c_-=c_+=1 and balanced propensity.

findings.issue: Notation reuses H for distinct objects: H(t0) is the least-favorable local radius, while H(O^S) and H_i are inverse-propensity instrument scores. This creates avoidable friction in the lower-bound and score-inversion sections.
findings.fix: Rename the least-favorable radius to h_max(t0) or a similar scalar notation, leaving H_i or H(O^S) for the score.

findings.issue: The sentence 'The formal derivations state their assumptions and conclusions explicitly.' appears as a standalone transition and is repeated in substance in the verification note. It adds little for the reader.
findings.fix: Remove the standalone sentence in the introduction or replace it with a concrete roadmap sentence naming the theorem groups and their role.

questions_for_authors: Which empirical or experimental designs motivated the uniform finite-cell class, and should readers view it as an exact design model or as a benchmark for discretized covariates?
Can the related-work section state explicitly how the expected-length rate here compares with the closest weak-LATE and transported-CACE procedures under their own assumptions?
